findings.title: hooks/lib/common.sh is installed and validated but never sourced by any hook
findings.detail: No production hook sources common.sh. The grep confirms zero calls to SCRIPT_DIR_OF, claude_logs_dir, ensure_logs_dir, or extract_jq_field anywhere in hooks/*.sh. log-tool-calls.sh resolves its own script dir inline (3 lines, lines 13-17). log-rotate.sh hardcodes LOG_DIR directly. The bash safety hooks need no path resolution. common.sh was created as TDD scaffolding in Task 4 of the plan but was never wired into any of the hooks written in subsequent tasks. It is installed as a symlink into ~/.claude/hooks/lib/, checked by validate.sh, documented in README and HOOKS.md, and tested for existence in test-install.sh — but it is dead at runtime. A maintainer reading a future hook will find common.sh, assume it is the canonical way to resolve paths, source it, and inherit a 30-line macOS/GNU portability shim they never needed.
findings.recommendation: Either delete common.sh and remove it from validate.sh's symlink check list, or immediately migrate log-tool-calls.sh's inline SCRIPT_DIR resolution to use SCRIPT_DIR_OF so the library earns its keep. If the plan is to use it for future hooks, a one-line comment in every hook that does its own path resolution (/* see hooks/lib/common.sh for a portable alternative */) would at least signal the intent. As-is, it is a dead file with a living installation footprint.

findings.title: log_tool_call.py duplicates redact.py and jsonl-write.py verbatim with a synchronization contract in comments
findings.location: hooks/lib/log_tool_call.py lines 30-96 vs hooks/lib/redact.py and hooks/lib/jsonl-write.py
findings.detail: _PATTERNS in log_tool_call.py (lines 32-50) is a line-for-line copy of _PATTERNS in redact.py (lines 25-55). The _truncate_output function in log_tool_call.py (lines 71-96) is a line-for-line copy of _truncate_output in jsonl-write.py (lines 25-58). The _atomic_append function (lines 99-106) reimplements the same O_APPEND write in jsonl-write.py (lines 79-88). The author acknowledges this with 'kept in sync with hooks/lib/redact.py' and 'kept in sync with hooks/lib/jsonl-write.py' comments. The perf rationale is documented: replacing 5 process forks (bash wrapper + 4 jq calls + redact.py + jsonl-write.py) with a single python3 invocation. That rationale is real and measurable. However the maintenance cost is equally real: any change to a redaction pattern must be made in two files; any fix to truncation logic must be made in two files; the test suite only exercises redact.py directly (test-redaction.sh), not the copy inside log_tool_call.py. A security fix to redact.py that misses log_tool_call.py has already happened once in this PR (the Authorization-header partial-leak fix caught by adversarial review). The synchronization comment is an acknowledgment that the duplication is a known liability, not a justification for it.
findings.recommendation: Extract _PATTERNS, _redact_value, _truncate_output, and _atomic_append into a single hooks/lib/_log_utils.py (no CLI entry point, importable only). redact.py and jsonl-write.py become thin wrappers that import from it; log_tool_call.py does the same. The single python3 invocation perf win is fully preserved. The synchronization risk is eliminated. The test suite exercises one copy and all callers benefit. If the extraction feels premature, at a minimum add a test case to test-redaction.sh that exercises the _PATTERNS copy inside log_tool_call.py directly (e.g., pipe a fixture through log_tool_call.py pre and grep the output log for the redaction markers).

findings.title: redact.py and jsonl-write.py have no callers in the active production path
findings.detail: The live logging pipeline is: log-tool-calls.sh -> log_tool_call.py. Neither redact.py nor jsonl-write.py is invoked anywhere in production hook execution. They are installed as symlinks into ~/.claude/hooks/lib/ and appear in validate.sh's symlink check. Their only active callers are tests/test-redaction.sh (exercises redact.py standalone) and no test exercises jsonl-write.py as a standalone callable at all. A developer asked to 'update the logging pipeline' will find four files (log-tool-calls.sh, log_tool_call.py, redact.py, jsonl-write.py) and need to determine which are live. The README points to redact.py as the canonical patterns reference ('Patterns in hooks/lib/redact.py'), which is accurate but incomplete since the live path reads from log_tool_call.py's copy. This is a direct consequence of M-02: the decomposed files were the design but were superseded by the consolidated file without being removed.
findings.recommendation: If log_tool_call.py remains the consolidated implementation (keeping the perf win), add a prominent note to redact.py and jsonl-write.py headers: 'NOTE: Not called by the active logging pipeline. log_tool_call.py contains an inlined copy of this logic for performance. Update both files in sync, or see M-02 in the maintainability review.' Update the README logging section to say 'canonical pattern definitions are in hooks/lib/redact.py but log_tool_call.py contains an inlined copy — see that file for the live implementation.' Or proceed with the shared module approach from M-02.

findings.title: block-rm-rf.sh and block-push-main.sh are functionally subsumed by safety-block.sh but remain wired as active hooks
findings.detail: All three hooks fire on every Bash tool call. safety-block.sh's rm-rf check (line 24) matches a strict superset of block-rm-rf.sh's check (root/home targets only vs any rm -rf). safety-block.sh's force-push checks (lines 59-64) match a strict superset of block-push-main.sh's check (handles --force, --force-with-lease, -f, and multiple branch name variants vs only 'git push origin main/master'). Every command that block-rm-rf.sh or block-push-main.sh would block is also blocked by safety-block.sh. The legacy hooks add a second independent check, meaning a false-positive block is more likely if any of the three regex approaches has a bug. They also add two extra process forks per Bash tool call. The comment in safety-block.sh header ('existing hooks/block-rm-rf.sh and hooks/block-push-main.sh remain wired up alongside this one for back-compat') names the intent but 'back-compat' is not a meaningful property here: this is a personal global config, not a library with external consumers. There is no migration period for a single developer's machine.
findings.recommendation: Remove block-rm-rf.sh and block-push-main.sh from the PreToolUse hook array in settings.json. Keep the files in the repo (they are documented as opt-in legacy hooks) but stop wiring them. Update the README and HOOKS.md to mark them as 'superseded by safety-block.sh'. This removes two forks per Bash call, eliminates two redundant block paths, and makes the active hook set smaller and clearer. If the narrower block-rm-rf.sh check (any rm -rf, not just root/home) is intentional as an additional layer, that should be documented explicitly, but the current comments do not indicate this.

findings.title: install_settings jq merge expression uses $existing * $new (object merge) which silently drops hooks from existing settings
findings.detail: The jq merge expression uses $existing * $new which in jq performs a recursive object merge where $new wins on key conflicts. For .hooks, this means if the existing ~/.claude/settings.json has a PreToolUse array with entries not in the repo's settings.json, those entries are silently dropped after merge (the line .hooks = ($existing.hooks // {}) * ($new.hooks // {}) on line 146 overwrites the existing hooks object with a merge where repo hooks win). The expression then special-cases .permissions.deny and .permissions.allow with array union, but .hooks gets standard jq object merge semantics with no documentation that this is intentional. A developer adding a project-specific hook directly to ~/.claude/settings.json will lose it on the next install --force or settings component run. The function name install_settings and the comment 'jq-merged into ~/.claude/settings.json (preserves existing enabledPlugins...)' do not mention what is not preserved.
findings.recommendation: Either change the merge to append hooks arrays (analogous to the permissions.allow/deny union), or add an explicit comment at the jq expression documenting that .hooks from the repo wins entirely on key conflict and that per-hook-type arrays are not merged. The install help text should warn: 'custom hooks added directly to ~/.claude/settings.json outside this repo will be overwritten — manage them through this repo or ~/.claude/settings.local.json if that pattern is supported.'

residual_risks.description: The 'kept in sync' comment on log_tool_call.py's _PATTERNS is a synchronization contract that has already been violated once (Authorization-header fix). Any future addition to redact.py's _PATTERNS that is not mirrored in log_tool_call.py will silently leak secrets to the JSONL log while redact.py's tests continue to pass. There is no automated check that the two copies are identical.

block-push-main.sh's regex (line 16: 'git push [a-zA-Z_-]+ (main|master)') does not require --force and blocks all pushes to main, including non-force pushes. safety-block.sh's force-push checks only block --force/-f. These two hooks have different semantics: one enforces 'no direct push to main at all', the other enforces 'no force-push anywhere'. Running both simultaneously creates an ambiguous block message: a plain 'git push origin main' from a feature branch will be blocked by block-push-main.sh with 'Use feature branches' but allowed by safety-block.sh. If block-push-main.sh is removed per M-04, this broader 'no direct push to main' policy is lost.

testing_gaps.description: test-redaction.sh exercises hooks/lib/redact.py directly but does not verify that hooks/lib/log_tool_call.py applies the same patterns. A secret that bypasses the copy in log_tool_call.py would not be caught. A test that pipes a fixture containing each secret pattern through 'hooks/log-tool-calls.sh pre' and greps the resulting JSONL line would close this gap.

No test verifies that block-rm-rf.sh and block-push-main.sh and safety-block.sh do not double-block a command or produce conflicting exit codes on the same input. The test-hooks.sh exercises each hook in isolation but not the settings.json hook chain order. If the hook runner short-circuits on first exit 2, the ordering matters for which error message Claude receives.

common.sh has no test that exercises it from a symlinked path (which is how it lives in ~/.claude/hooks/lib/). The SCRIPT_DIR_OF function's macOS-portable fallback (the cd/pwd path) is only reachable when both greadlink and GNU readlink are absent, which is the default macOS case without Homebrew coreutils. There is no test fixture that invokes SCRIPT_DIR_OF through a symlink from a non-repo path to verify the fallback works correctly.
